title: If and Unless
overview: Say exactly what has to be true before something else can happen. Use unless, provided, as long as and otherwise, keep the future out of the condition half, and choose a future form that matches the evidence you actually have. Then read somebody else's conditions and work out what they really require.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a lease, a language guide and a set of hire terms.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Set a clear condition on something you agree to
Say what will happen if a condition is not met
Warn somebody, and say what follows if they ignore it
Talk about the future without sounding more certain than you are
Say whether you mean people in general or one particular group
Turn an action into a thing, so you can write about it briefly
Work out what a contract actually requires you to do
lectureScript:
This unit is about conditions, and it is one of the most practical in the whole level.
Conditions are where money lives. In a lease, in a hire agreement, in a job offer, the conditions are the part that decides what actually happens.

You already have if, in both its shapes.
If you heat ice, it melts. If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
Those still work, and this unit does not repeat them.
What it adds is the other words, and each of them says something if cannot.

The most important is unless, and there is one thing to get right about it.
Unless means if not. Both words, folded into one.
So I will not sign unless they put it in writing is correct.
I will not sign unless they do not put it in writing says the opposite of what you mean, because the not is in there twice and two negatives cancel.
There is a test that never fails. Replace unless with if not and read it again. If it still means what you wanted, you were right.

Then provided, and this one is worth real attention, because the reading in this unit turns on it.
If says here is a condition. Provided says here is the ONE condition, and nothing else will do.
A firm in the reading had a lease that said the landlord would maintain the heating provided it was serviced annually by an approved engineer.
They had it serviced. They did not use an approved engineer, because nobody told them there was a list.
The landlord refused, and he was within his rights, and they were three weeks without heating.
Nobody missed the clause. They all read it. They read provided as though it meant if.
As long as does the same job as provided, less formally.
Otherwise carries the whole negative condition by itself, in a new sentence. Book early. Otherwise you will not get a place.
And assuming and suppose open a case you are not sure about. Assuming the parts arrive, we will finish on Friday.

The second pattern is a rule you have half of, and it is worth stating properly because it is one rule and not six.
After if, unless, when, until, as soon as, provided, as long as and assuming, you do not use will.
If it rains tomorrow, I will take the bus.
Both halves are about the future. Only one of them says so.
English marks the future once, and it never marks it in the half with the condition word.
There is one exception worth knowing. When has a second use, meaning at what time, and there will is allowed.
I do not know when they will reply is correct, because that when is a question, not a condition.
When they reply, I will tell you takes the present, because that when is a condition.
Same word. Two jobs. Only one of them blocks the will.

The third pattern is about how certain you sound, and most learners never think about it.
Level 2 had you choose between futures by what they mean. This chooses by what evidence you have.
Will is an opinion or a prediction with nothing in particular behind it. I think it will rain.
Going to claims evidence. You can see the clouds, or you already decided last week.
The present continuous means it is arranged. There is a time, and somebody else knows about it.
And is likely to, is due to and is about to are the careful middle.
The test is one question. Why do you believe it? The answer picks the form.
And there is a real cost to getting it wrong. Saying it is going to be fine when you have no reason at all makes you sound surer than you are, and people remember that.

The fourth pattern cleans up something you have been half-doing for two levels.
You know some, any, many, much, a few, both, all, fewer, less, either and neither.
What nobody has given you is the rule that governs all of them, and it is the word of.
Most people never complain is about people in general. No of, no the.
Most of the people in the room had already left is about one particular group. Of, and then the.
Both sentences are correct English and they are different claims.
Most of people is the error, and it is extremely common, because it sits exactly between the two right answers.
The of and the the travel together. You cannot have one without the other.

The last pattern is the one that will grow your writing fastest.
Level 2 built two nouns for you: kindness, and sunshine. This gives you the machinery.
Decide becomes decision. Prevent becomes prevention. Agree becomes agreement. Possible becomes possibility.
Why bother? Because a noun can be the subject of a sentence, and a verb in the middle of a clause cannot.
They decided late, and it cost us becomes the late decision cost us.
Shorter, and the idea is now a thing you can point at and build on.
Watch the spellings, because they shift. Apply becomes application, with the y turning into an i.
Refer becomes reference, and loses one of its r's.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: Something that happens as a result of something else.
words.example: The consequence of the delay was a lost contract.
practice: Every decision has a consequence, whether you see it or not.
Consequence takes of: the consequence OF the delay.
As a consequence means therefore.
Consequently is the adverb.
words.tutor: Name a consequence of something. Ask the tutor to check you said consequence OF.

words.meaning: The way something finally turns out.
words.example: The outcome was better than anybody expected.
practice: We will not know the outcome until March.
An outcome is the end result; a consequence is caused by something.
Outcome is neutral: it can be good or bad.
The outcome of the meeting, not the outcome for.
words.tutor: Describe an outcome. Ask the tutor whether outcome or consequence was right.

words.meaning: A change produced by something else.
words.example: The new rule had almost no effect.
practice: The effect on morale was immediate.
Effect is the noun; affect is the verb.
It has an effect ON something.
In effect means in practice.
words.tutor: Say what effect something had. Ask the tutor whether you used effect or affect.

words.meaning: A strong effect, especially a sudden one.
words.example: The closure had a real impact on the town.
practice: The impact was felt within weeks.
Impact is stronger than effect, and takes on.
It is also a verb, though many people dislike that use.
A high-impact change is one people notice.
words.tutor: Describe an impact. Ask the tutor whether impact was too strong a word.

words.meaning: To cause something to start, suddenly.
words.example: The failed inspection triggered a full review.
practice: A single complaint triggered the whole investigation.
Trigger suits a sudden start, not a slow one.
It is also a noun: the trigger for the review.
Triggered by is the common passive form.
words.tutor: Say what triggered something. Ask the tutor whether trigger suited the speed of it.

words.meaning: To stop something from happening.
words.example: Better checks would have prevented it.
practice: Nothing prevents you from asking.
Prevent takes from before an -ing form.
Prevention is the noun.
Prevent is about stopping before; stop can be during.
words.tutor: Say what would have prevented a problem. Ask the tutor to check the word after prevent.

words.meaning: Probably going to happen.
words.example: It is likely to rain before six.
practice: A delay is likely, so plan for one.
Likely takes to before a verb.
It is an adjective, not an adverb, in careful English.
More likely than not means over half.
words.tutor: Say what is likely. Ask the tutor to check you used to and a plain verb.

words.meaning: Probably not going to happen.
words.example: They are unlikely to reply before Monday.
practice: It is unlikely, but not impossible.
Unlikely also takes to.
Highly unlikely is the usual strengthener, not very.
It is the plain opposite of likely.
words.tutor: Say what is unlikely. Ask the tutor whether unlikely or impossible was right.

words.meaning: Likely to be true or to happen.
words.example: The probable cause was water.
practice: A probable outcome is one you would bet on.
Probable is commoner before a noun: the probable cause.
Probably is the adverb and is far commoner in speech.
Probable is stronger than possible.
words.tutor: Name a probable cause of something. Ask the tutor whether probable or possible was right.

words.meaning: Certain to happen, and impossible to prevent.
words.example: Some delay was inevitable.
practice: It was inevitable that somebody would complain.
Inevitable is already absolute, so no very.
Inevitably is the adverb.
It sits at the far end of the likely scale.
words.tutor: Say what was inevitable. Ask the tutor to check you did not say very inevitable.

words.meaning: Something that might happen.
words.example: There is a possibility of a strike.
practice: We should consider every possibility.
Possibility takes of before a noun, and that before a clause.
A possibility is weaker than a probability.
Its adjective is possible.
words.tutor: Name a possibility. Ask the tutor to check the word after possibility.

words.meaning: The likelihood of something happening; also an opportunity.
words.example: There is a good chance it will be approved.
practice: The chances of that are small.
Chance of a noun, or chance that plus a clause.
It also means opportunity: a chance to travel.
By chance means accidentally.
words.starter: There is a good chance that …
words.tutor: Say what there is a good chance of. Ask the tutor which of the two meanings you used.

words.meaning: Something that must be true before something else can happen.
words.example: They agreed, on one condition.
practice: The condition is that you finish by Friday.
On condition that is the full phrase.
Condition also means the state of a thing: in good condition.
Conditional is the adjective.
words.tutor: State a condition. Ask the tutor to check the phrase on condition that.

words.meaning: Only if; on the condition that.
words.example: You may start provided the site is clear.
practice: Provided that and provided mean the same.
Provided is more formal than if, and stronger.
It says this is the ONE thing that must be true.
Providing also works and is slightly less formal.
words.tutor: Set a condition using provided. Ask the tutor whether provided or if was better.

words.meaning: If not; in the other case.
words.example: Book early. Otherwise you will not get a place.
practice: Otherwise carries the whole negative condition by itself.
It usually starts its own sentence.
It can also mean in other respects: otherwise it is fine.
Otherwise saves you writing a second if clause.
words.tutor: Use otherwise to warn somebody. Ask the tutor to check both halves.

words.meaning: If we take it as true that.
words.example: Assuming the parts arrive, we will finish on Friday.
practice: Assuming that and assuming mean the same.
It flags that you are not certain of the condition.
Assume is the verb; assumption is the noun.
Assuming is more tentative than provided.
words.tutor: Make a plan using assuming. Ask the tutor whether the uncertainty came across.

words.meaning: To imagine something as true, in order to think about it.
words.example: Suppose the parts do not arrive. What then?
practice: Supposing it rains, what is the plan?
Suppose and supposing both open an imagined case.
I suppose so is a weak agreement.
Supposed to means expected to.
words.tutor: Open an imagined case with suppose. Ask the tutor to check the question that followed.

words.meaning: To be decided by something else.
words.example: It depends on the weather.
practice: Everything depends on whether they reply.
Depend always takes on, with no exception.
It depends is a complete answer in speech.
Dependent is the adjective; dependant is a person.
words.tutor: Say what something depends on. Ask the tutor to check you said depend ON.

words.meaning: To tell somebody about a danger before it happens.
words.example: I warned them the floor was wet.
practice: She warned us not to sign it.
Warn somebody ABOUT a thing, or warn somebody TO do something.
Warning is the noun.
You warn before; you tell off afterwards.
words.tutor: Warn somebody about something. Ask the tutor to check the form after warn.

words.meaning: To say you will cause harm; or to be about to happen.
words.example: The supplier threatened to stop deliveries.
practice: Rain threatened all afternoon.
Threaten takes to before a verb.
Threat is the noun.
A threatened species is one at risk.
words.tutor: Say what somebody threatened to do. Ask the tutor whether threaten was too strong.

words.meaning: To make certain that something happens.
words.example: Please ensure the gate is locked.
practice: Ensure that everybody signs in.
Ensure is make certain; insure is about insurance.
It takes that plus a clause.
Ensure is formal: in speech you would say make sure.
words.tutor: Write an instruction with ensure. Ask the tutor whether you meant ensure or insure.

words.meaning: To fix something firmly; or to succeed in getting it.
words.example: Secure the ladder before you climb.
practice: She secured a place on the course.
Secure is also an adjective: the load is secure.
Security is the noun.
The two meanings are far apart: fix, and obtain.
words.tutor: Use secure in an instruction. Ask the tutor which of the two meanings you used.

words.meaning: A second thing kept in case the first one fails.
words.example: There is no backup if the generator stops.
practice: Always keep a backup of anything that matters.
Backup as a noun is one word; back up as a verb is two.
A backup plan is the same idea.
It also means extra help: we called for backup.
words.tutor: Say what has no backup. Ask the tutor whether you spelled backup as one word.

words.meaning: A plan for something that might go wrong.
words.example: We have a contingency if the parts are late.
practice: A contingency plan is written before you need it.
Contingency money is money set aside for problems.
It is pronounced con-TIN-jen-see.
A contingency is for a possibility, not a certainty.
words.tutor: Describe a contingency. Ask the tutor whether contingency or backup was right.

words.meaning: To think about something carefully before deciding.
words.example: We considered three suppliers.
practice: Have you considered moving the date?
Consider takes an -ing form, never to.
Consideration is the noun.
All things considered means having weighed everything.
words.tutor: Say what you considered. Ask the tutor to check the form after consider.

words.meaning: To compare the good and bad sides before deciding.
words.example: You have to weigh the cost against the delay.
practice: We weighed both options for a week.
Weigh takes against for the comparison.
Weigh up is the same thing, slightly more informal.
It also means to measure weight.
words.tutor: Weigh two things against each other. Ask the tutor to check you used against.

words.meaning: To pause before acting, because you are unsure.
words.example: I hesitated, and the place went to somebody else.
practice: Do not hesitate to ask.
Hesitate takes to before a verb.
Hesitation is the noun.
Without hesitation means immediately.
words.tutor: Say why you hesitated. Ask the tutor to check the form after hesitate.

words.meaning: To decide firmly and bind yourself to it.
words.example: I am not ready to commit to a date.
practice: Once you commit, it is difficult to change.
Commit takes to, and after to comes a noun or an -ing form.
Commitment is the noun, with two m's and two t's.
Committed also means dedicated.
words.starter: I am not ready to commit to …
words.tutor: Say what you are not ready to commit to. Ask the tutor to check the form after to.

words.meaning: Another choice you could take instead.
words.example: There was no realistic alternative.
practice: The alternative is to wait until spring.
Alternative takes to: an alternative TO waiting.
It is also an adjective: an alternative route.
Strictly, an alternative is one of two.
words.tutor: Name an alternative. Ask the tutor to check the word after alternative.

grammar.title: Unless, provided, otherwise: saying the condition a different way
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you if, in both its shapes.
If you heat ice, it melts. If it rains, I will take the bus.
Those two still work. What this card adds is the other words that set a
condition, each of which says something if cannot say on its own.
grammar.rule:
UNLESS = if not. One word instead of two.
I will not sign unless they put it in writing.
  = I will not sign if they do not put it in writing.
Unless is NEVER followed by not. The not is already inside it.

PROVIDED (THAT) = only if, and this is the one thing that matters.
You may start provided the site is clear.
It is stronger and more formal than if.

AS LONG AS = the same as provided, and less formal.
You can borrow it as long as you bring it back.

OTHERWISE = if not, carrying the whole condition by itself.
Book early. Otherwise you will not get a place.
It starts a new sentence, so there is no if clause at all.

ASSUMING / SUPPOSE = I am not sure this is true, but let us say it is.
Assuming the parts arrive, we will finish on Friday.
Suppose they do not arrive. What then?
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Rewrite with unless: I will not sign if they do not put it in writing.
1. Find the if plus not. if they do NOT put it in writing.
2. unless already means if not, so it replaces both words.
3. Take the not out. Leaving it in would make the sentence mean the opposite.
Answer: I will not sign unless they put it in writing.
Notice the other half keeps its own not. Only the if clause changed.
grammar.mistake:
unless not is the error, and it reverses your meaning.
No: I will not sign unless they do not put it in writing.
Yes: I will not sign unless they put it in writing.
unless already contains the not. Saying it twice cancels it.
grammar.tip: unless = if not, in one word. Never put not after it.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one using the word in brackets.
1. I will not sign if they do not put it in writing. (unless)
2. You may start if the site is clear, and only then. (provided)
3. If you do not book early, you will not get a place. (otherwise)
4. You can borrow it if you bring it back. (as long as)
5. If the parts do not arrive, we cannot finish. (unless)
Now correct these two.
6. I will not go unless they do not invite me.
7. Unless it will rain, we will start at eight.
grammar.answers:
1. I will not sign unless they put it in writing.
2. You may start provided the site is clear.
3. Book early. Otherwise you will not get a place.
4. You can borrow it as long as you bring it back.
5. We cannot finish unless the parts arrive.
6. I will not go unless they invite me. (the not was doubled)
7. Unless it rains, we will start at eight. (no will in the condition)
Number 7 is the rule from the next card, arriving early.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: No will after if, when or unless
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 taught this for when and until: when the parcel comes, I will ring you.
The rule is wider than that unit could show, and it catches every condition
word in the card before this one. It is worth stating once, properly.
grammar.rule:
The future goes in the MAIN half only. The condition half stays present.

If it rains tomorrow, I WILL take the bus.
Unless they reply by Friday, I WILL ring them.
As soon as the parts arrive, we WILL start.
Provided the site is clear, you MAY begin.
Assuming nothing goes wrong, it WILL be finished by six.

Every one of those is about the future. Only one half says so.

The words this covers:
if, unless, when, until, as soon as, provided, as long as, assuming, before, after

Careful: when has a second use where will IS allowed.
I do not know when they will reply.  (this when means at what time,
                                      and it is a question, not a condition)
When they reply, I will tell you.    (this when is a condition)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose the form: Unless it ___ (rain), we will start at eight.
1. Which half is this? The condition half, because unless opens it.
2. The condition half never takes will, however future the meaning.
3. So use the present simple: rains.
Answer: Unless it rains, we will start at eight.
The will has already been used, correctly, in the other half.
grammar.mistake:
Learners put will in both halves, because both halves are about the future.
No: If it will rain, I will take the bus.
Yes: If it rains, I will take the bus.
English marks the future once, and the condition half is not where it goes.
grammar.tip: One future per sentence, and it goes in the half WITHOUT the condition word.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form.
1. Unless it ___ (rain), we will start at eight.
2. If the parts ___ (arrive) tomorrow, we will finish on Friday.
3. As soon as she ___ (ring), I will let you know.
4. Provided the site ___ (be) clear, you may begin.
5. I do not know when they ___ (reply).
6. When they ___ (reply), I will tell you.
Now correct these.
7. If it will rain, I will take the bus.
8. I will ring you as soon as I will hear anything.
grammar.answers:
1. rains  2. arrive  3. rings  4. is  5. will reply  6. reply
7. If it rains, I will take the bus.
8. I will ring you as soon as I hear anything.
Number 5 is the exception: that when means at what time, so will is correct.
Number 6 is the same word doing the other job, so it takes the present.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: How sure are you? Letting the future form carry your evidence
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 had you choose between four futures by what they MEAN.
This card chooses by something else: how much evidence you have.
Each form tells the listener where your confidence comes from, and
choosing the wrong one makes you sound more or less certain than you are.
grammar.rule:
WILL — a prediction, an opinion, or a decision made as you speak.
I think it will rain. I will help you. It will be fine.
Evidence: none in particular. This is what you reckon.

GOING TO — you can SEE the evidence, or you already decided.
Look at those clouds. It is going to rain.
We are going to move the date. (decided before now)
Evidence: something in front of you, or a decision already taken.

PRESENT CONTINUOUS — it is arranged, with a time and usually a person.
I am meeting them on Tuesday.
Evidence: a diary. Somebody else knows about it too.

IS LIKELY TO / IS DUE TO / IS ABOUT TO — the careful middle.
It is likely to rain.        (probable, hedged)
The train is due to arrive at six. (a timetable says so)
It is about to start.        (any second now)

The test: ask yourself WHY you believe it. The answer chooses the form.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You look out of the window and the sky is black. Which form?
1. Ask why you believe it. Because you can see the clouds.
2. Visible evidence in front of you is going to, not will.
Answer: It is going to rain.
I think it will rain would be right if somebody asked your opinion indoors,
with no window and no clouds to point at.
grammar.mistake:
going to is not just an informal will. It claims evidence.
Weak: I think it is going to be fine. (on what basis?)
Better: I think it will be fine. (an opinion, honestly labelled)
Using going to with no evidence makes you sound surer than you are.
grammar.tip: Ask why you believe it. No reason: will. Something you can point at: going to. A diary: continuous.
grammar.practice:
Choose the best future form and say why.
1. The sky is black. It ___ rain.
2. Somebody asks your opinion about next week's weather. I think it ___ rain.
3. You have an appointment on Tuesday at ten. I ___ the client on Tuesday.
4. The timetable says six o'clock. The train ___ arrive at six.
5. The phone rings and you stand up. I ___ get it.
6. You decided last week to move the date. We ___ move the date.
grammar.answers:
1. is going to rain (you can see the evidence)
2. will rain (an opinion, with nothing to point at)
3. am meeting (arranged, in a diary, and somebody else knows)
4. is due to arrive (a timetable says so)
5. will get it (decided as you speak)
6. are going to move it (decided before now)
Numbers 5 and 6 are the pair worth studying: will is decided NOW,
going to was decided EARLIER.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Most of the people, or most people? The quantifiers Level 2 left out
grammar.explanation:
You already have some, any, many, much, a few, a little, both, all, fewer,
less, either, neither and plenty. That is a great many.
What no unit has given you is the OF rule, which decides them all, and the
handful of quantifiers that are still missing.
grammar.rule:
THE OF RULE, which is the whole card.

Talking about people or things IN GENERAL: no of, no the.
Most people never complain.
Few applicants read the whole form.
Several suppliers raised their prices.

Talking about a PARTICULAR group: of, and then the, my, these, them.
Most OF THE people in the room had already left.
Few OF THE applicants we saw were suitable.
Several OF THEM raised their prices.

So: most people (everybody in the world)
    most of the people (that specific group)
Both are correct, and they mean different things.

The ones still missing from your set:
the majority of   most of — formal, and always takes of
hardly any        almost none
a great deal of   a lot of, for things you cannot count
none of           not one, and it takes of
no                none, and it takes NO of: no applicants

none of takes a singular verb in careful writing:
None of the parts HAS arrived.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: ___ never complain. (you mean people in general)
1. Is this a general statement or a particular group? General.
2. General means no of and no the.
Answer: Most people never complain.
Most of the people never complain would mean a specific group you have in mind,
which is a smaller and different claim.
grammar.mistake:
The of goes in when, and only when, you name a particular group.
No: Most of people never complain.
Yes: Most people never complain.  or  Most of THE people never complain.
of and the travel together. You cannot have one without the other.
grammar.tip: General? No of. A particular group? of, and then the.
grammar.practice:
Choose most people or most of the people, and so on.
1. ___ never complain. (people in general)
2. ___ in the room had already left. (that room)
3. ___ read the whole form. (applicants in general — use few)
4. ___ we interviewed were suitable. (the ones we saw — use few)
5. ___ the parts ___ (have) arrived. (not one — use none)
6. ___ applicants applied before the deadline. (not any — use no)
Now correct these.
7. Most of people never complain.
8. The majority people agreed.
grammar.answers:
1. Most people  2. Most of the people  3. Few applicants
4. Few of the applicants  5. None of the parts has arrived  6. No applicants
7. Most people never complain. (or: most of THE people)
8. The majority OF people agreed. (the majority always takes of)
Number 5 takes a singular verb in careful writing, because none means not one.
Number 6 is the odd one: no never takes of.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Decide becomes decision: building the noun you need
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 made two nouns for you: kindness from kind, and sunshine from sun.
This card gives you the machinery, so you can build the noun for almost any
verb or adjective you already know. It is the single fastest way to grow
your written vocabulary.
grammar.rule:
FROM A VERB:
-tion / -sion   decide -> decision, prevent -> prevention, apply -> application
-ment           agree -> agreement, assess -> assessment, commit -> commitment
-ance / -ence   depend -> dependence, refer -> reference
-al             approve -> approval, arrive -> arrival

FROM AN ADJECTIVE:
-ness           aware -> awareness, ready -> readiness
-ity            possible -> possibility, able -> ability
-ce             different -> difference, absent -> absence

Spellings that shift as you add the ending:
apply -> application  (y becomes i)
refer -> reference    (one r, not two)
decide -> decision    (the de becomes s)

Why it matters: a noun lets you make the idea the SUBJECT of a sentence.
They decided late, and it cost us.
The late decision cost us.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Rewrite with a noun: They decided late, and it cost us.
1. Find the verb carrying the idea: decided.
2. Its noun is decision, with the de becoming s.
3. Move late in front of it: the late decision.
4. That phrase is now the subject of the whole sentence.
Answer: The late decision cost us.
Shorter, and the idea has become a thing you can point at.
grammar.mistake:
The ending is not predictable, and the spelling often shifts.
No: applyation, decidesion, referrence.
Yes: application, decision, reference.
When you are not sure, write the word out and look at it. Wrong spellings usually look wrong.
grammar.tip: Learn the noun with the verb, as one item, and watch the spelling shift.
grammar.practice:
Write the noun for each word.
1. decide   2. prevent   3. agree   4. apply   5. depend
6. possible 7. aware     8. refer   9. approve 10. commit
Now rewrite each sentence so the idea becomes the subject.
11. They decided late, and it cost us.
12. They delayed, and that triggered the review.
grammar.answers:
1. decision  2. prevention  3. agreement  4. application  5. dependence
6. possibility  7. awareness  8. reference  9. approval  10. commitment
11. The late decision cost us.
12. The delay triggered the review.
Watch 4 (y becomes i), 8 (one r, not two) and 10 (one t, unlike committed).
9 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Clause Nobody Read
readings.setting: A small firm, told a year afterwards
readings.passage:
We signed the lease in March, and the trouble started in November.
There was one clause about the heating, and none of us read it properly.
It said the landlord would maintain the system provided it was serviced annually by an approved engineer.
We had it serviced. We did not use an approved engineer, because nobody told us there was a list.
So when the boiler failed, the landlord refused, and he was entitled to.
The consequence was three weeks without heating and a bill we had not budgeted for.
Looking back, the mistake was not missing the clause. We all saw it.
The mistake was reading provided as if it meant if, which is nearly the same and not the same at all.
If says here is a condition. Provided says here is the ONE condition, and nothing else will do.
I read leases differently now. I look for unless, provided and otherwise first, before anything else.
Those three words are where the money usually is.
Assuming you find them early, most of the rest is straightforward.

readings.title: Why Unless Never Takes Not
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passage:
Unless means if not. Both words, in one word.
That is the whole rule, and almost every mistake with unless comes from forgetting it.
I will not sign unless they put it in writing is correct.
I will not sign unless they do not put it in writing says the opposite of what the speaker means.
The not has been used twice, and two negatives cancel.
There is a simple test. Replace unless with if not and read the sentence again.
If it still means what you wanted, the unless was right.
A second thing to watch is the tense.
Unless it rains, we will start at eight is correct.
Unless it will rain is not, however clearly the sentence is about tomorrow.
English marks the future once, in the half without the condition word.
This catches if, when, until, as soon as, provided and unless alike.
It is one rule, not six, and it is worth learning as one.

readings.title: Hire Terms: Conditions of Use
readings.setting: The back of a tool hire agreement
readings.passage:
CONDITIONS OF HIRE

1. Equipment is released only on production of photographic identification.
2. The hirer may extend the period provided notice is given before 4pm on the due date.
3. Unless the equipment is returned by the due time, a further full day is charged.
4. The deposit is refunded in full as long as the equipment is returned clean and undamaged.
5. Damage must be reported on return. Otherwise the hirer is charged the full replacement cost.
6. None of the items may be taken outside the mainland without written consent.

If the equipment fails through no fault of the hirer, the hire charge is cancelled
and a replacement is offered where one is available.

The majority of disputes arise from condition 3. Please note the time, not only the date.
Assuming the equipment is returned on time and clean, no further charge is made.

comprehension.q: What condition did the lease put on the landlord maintaining the heating?
comprehension.a: That it was serviced annually by an approved engineer.
comprehension.why: The clause is quoted in the third line.

comprehension.q: The firm had the system serviced. Why did the landlord still refuse?
comprehension.a: Because the engineer was not on the approved list.
comprehension.why: Provided named the one condition, and it was not met in full.

comprehension.q: What difference does the writer draw between if and provided?
comprehension.a: If gives a condition; provided gives the only condition, and nothing else will do.
comprehension.why: Stated directly in the ninth line.

comprehension.q: What does the writer now do first when reading a lease?
comprehension.a: Look for unless, provided and otherwise.
comprehension.why: The writer says those three words are where the money usually is.

comprehension.q: What test does the article give for checking a sentence with unless?
comprehension.a: Replace unless with if not and read it again.

comprehension.q: Why is 'unless they do not put it in writing' wrong?
comprehension.a: Because the not is used twice, and two negatives cancel each other.

comprehension.q: How many rules does the article say the tense point actually is?
comprehension.a: One rule, covering if, when, until, as soon as, provided and unless alike.
comprehension.why: The last two lines say so, and say it is worth learning as one.

comprehension.q: You return the equipment two hours after the due time. What happens?
comprehension.a: A further full day is charged.
comprehension.why: Condition 3, and the note at the foot says this causes most disputes.

comprehension.q: You want to keep the equipment another day. What must you do, and by when?
comprehension.a: Give notice before 4pm on the due date.
comprehension.why: Condition 2 uses provided to name the one condition.

comprehension.q: The equipment breaks down and it was not your fault. What are you entitled to?
comprehension.a: The hire charge is cancelled, and a replacement if one is available.
comprehension.why: The paragraph below the numbered conditions.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Five conditions you would set
speaking.instructions:
You are lending somebody something valuable. Set five conditions aloud.
Use a different condition word each time: unless, provided, as long as, otherwise, assuming.
A model, so you can hear the shape:
You can borrow it as long as you bring it back on Sunday.
I will not lend it unless you insure it.
You may use it provided you read the instructions first.
Do not leave it outside. Otherwise it will rust.
Assuming nothing goes wrong, you can keep it for a week.
Tap the mic. Say your five conditions. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you use all five words?
Did any sentence put not after unless?
speaking.tutor: Say your five conditions and ask the tutor whether any of them meant the opposite of what you intended.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Where the voice falls in a two-part sentence
speaking.instructions:
A conditional sentence has two halves, and the voice treats them differently.
The first half RISES slightly and does not finish. The second half falls.
That rise is how a listener knows more is coming.
Listen and repeat. The arrow shows the voice.
If it rains tomorrow (up), I will take the bus (down).
Unless they reply by Friday (up), I will ring them (down).
Provided the site is clear (up), you may begin (down).
Now say the same three with the halves swapped round.
I will take the bus if it rains tomorrow.
Notice the rise disappears, because nothing is left hanging.
Tap the mic. Say all three pairs. Tap again and listen.
Check: in the first version, can you hear your voice stay up at the comma?
speaking.tutor: Say the three sentences both ways round and ask the tutor which order sounded more natural.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — How sure are you?
speaking.instructions:
For each situation, say a full sentence with the future form that fits your evidence.
1. The sky is black and you are looking at it.
2. Somebody asks your opinion about next week's weather.
3. You have an appointment on Tuesday at ten.
4. The timetable says the train comes at six.
5. The phone rings and you stand up.
6. You decided last week to move the date.
Models: It is going to rain. I think it will be fine. I am meeting them on Tuesday.
Tap the mic. Say all six. Tap again and listen.
Check: 1 and 6 take going to. 2 and 5 take will.
3 takes the present continuous, and 4 takes is due to.
speaking.tutor: Say your six sentences and ask the tutor whether you ever sounded surer than your evidence allowed.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: the clause about the heating
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
The lease said the landlord would maintain the system.
It said that provided the system was serviced every year by an approved engineer.
We did have it serviced, so we thought we had met the condition.
Nobody had told us there was a list of approved engineers, and ours was not on it.
When the boiler failed in November, the landlord refused, and he was within his rights.
We were three weeks without heating and the bill was not one we had budgeted for.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. What did the lease say the landlord would do?
2. What was the condition?
3. Which part of the condition did the firm fail?
4. What were the two consequences?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 maintain the heating system. 2 an annual service by an approved engineer.
3 the engineer was not approved. 4 three weeks with no heating, and an unbudgeted bill.
speaking.tutor: Retell the problem in three sentences and ask the tutor which detail mattered most.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Most people, or most of them?
speaking.instructions:
Say each sentence twice: once about people in general, once about a particular group.
Listen for the of appearing and disappearing.
1. most people / most of the people in this room
2. few applicants / few of the applicants we saw
3. none of the parts / no parts
4. the majority of people / the majority of them
Models:
Most people never complain. Most of the people in this room had already left.
Tap the mic. Say all four pairs as full sentences. Tap again and listen.
Check: did the of appear only when you named a particular group?
In number 4, did of appear BOTH times? It should: the majority always takes it.
speaking.tutor: Say your four pairs and ask the tutor whether any of went missing or appeared where it should not.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: a plan and what could go wrong
speaking.instructions:
Describe a plan, real or invented, and the conditions it depends on.
Speak for two minutes and cover these four, in this order:
what you intend to do
what it depends on
what you will do if that fails
what would make you give up altogether
Use at least three condition words and at least two different future forms.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you put will into a condition half by mistake?
Did your future forms match how certain you actually are?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your two minutes and ask where a condition word or a tense went wrong.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Six conditions of hire
writing.prompt:
Write six numbered conditions for hiring something out, in the style of Reading 3.
Use unless, provided, as long as and otherwise at least once each.
Every condition must say what happens if it is not met.
writing.model:
1. Equipment is released only on production of photographic identification.
2. The hirer may extend the period provided notice is given before 4pm.
3. Unless the equipment is returned by the due time, a further full day is charged.
4. The deposit is refunded as long as the equipment is returned clean.
5. Damage must be reported on return. Otherwise the full replacement cost is charged.
6. None of the items may be taken abroad without written consent.
writing.length: Six numbered conditions, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
unless, provided, as long as and otherwise each used at least once.
No not after unless.
Every condition states a consequence.
No will inside a condition half.
writing.support: Write each one as an if sentence first, then swap in the stronger word.
writing.extension: Add a seventh condition using none of, with the right singular verb.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A plan and its conditions
writing.prompt:
Write a short plan for something you intend to do.
Say what it depends on, what you will do if that fails, and what would stop you altogether.
Use at least three different future forms, matched to how certain you are.
writing.model:
I am starting the course in September; the place is already booked.
It depends on whether my hours are reduced, which I have asked for twice.
Assuming they agree, I will study on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
If they refuse, I am going to apply for the evening version instead.
Unless both options fall through, I will have started by Christmas.
Otherwise I will wait until next year, which is not the end of the world.
writing.criteria:
At least three different future forms, each matching the evidence you have.
At least three condition words.
No will inside a condition half.
The arranged item uses the present continuous, not will.
writing.support: Write the four parts as headings first, then one or two sentences under each.
writing.extension: Add a sentence with is likely to or is due to, and say why you chose it over will.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Turn the verbs into nouns
writing.prompt:
Below are six short sentences. Rewrite each one so the idea becomes the SUBJECT,
using a noun built from the verb or adjective.
a) They decided late, and it cost us.
b) They delayed, and that triggered the review.
c) We applied, and it was refused.
d) He was absent, and nobody noticed.
e) They agreed, and that settled it.
f) The system depends on one supplier, which is risky.
Then write two sentences of your own in the same style.
writing.model:
a) The late decision cost us.
b) The delay triggered the review.
c) Our application was refused.
d) His absence went unnoticed.
e) The agreement settled it.
f) The system's dependence on one supplier is risky.
writing.length: Six rewrites plus two of your own, about 70 to 100 words.
writing.criteria:
All six nouns correctly formed and correctly spelled.
In each rewrite, the noun phrase is the subject of the sentence.
Every rewrite is shorter than the original.
The two new sentences use nouns not already in the list.
writing.support: Write the verb and its noun side by side first, then build the sentence round the noun.
writing.extension: Take one of your own sentences and turn it back into two clauses. Say which you prefer and why.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A warning notice
writing.prompt:
Write a short notice warning people about a risk, with six lines.
Use otherwise once, unless once, and ensure once.
State the consequence every time, and do not use the word please more than once.
writing.model:
SCAFFOLD IN USE — NORTH SIDE
Do not pass beyond the barrier unless you are wearing a hard hat.
Please ensure the gate is closed behind you at all times.
Report any loose boarding to the site office on the day it is noticed.
Deliveries are accepted at the south entrance only.
Do not move the barriers. Otherwise the whole section must be re-inspected.
The scaffold is checked every seven days. The next check is due on the 14th.
writing.length: A six-line notice, about 60 to 90 words.
writing.criteria:
otherwise, unless and ensure each used once.
No not after unless.
Every instruction carries a consequence or a reason.
please appears at most once.
writing.support: Write the six risks first, then turn each into an instruction plus a consequence.
writing.extension: Add a line using a contingency, saying what happens if the check is missed.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Say the condition another way
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each one using the word in brackets.
1. I will not sign if they do not put it in writing. (unless)
2. You may start if the site is clear, and only then. (provided)
3. If you do not book early, you will not get a place. (otherwise)
4. You can borrow it if you bring it back. (as long as)
5. If the parts do not arrive, we cannot finish. (unless)
6. If we take it that nothing goes wrong, it will be done by six. (assuming)
Now correct these.
7. I will not go unless they do not invite me.
8. Unless it will rain, we will start at eight.
activities.answers:
1. I will not sign unless they put it in writing.
2. You may start provided the site is clear.
3. Book early. Otherwise you will not get a place.
4. You can borrow it as long as you bring it back.
5. We cannot finish unless the parts arrive.
6. Assuming nothing goes wrong, it will be done by six.
7. I will not go unless they invite me.  8. Unless it rains, we will start at eight.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For every unless you write, replace it with if not and read the sentence back. It must still mean what you meant.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Which half takes the future?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. Unless it ___ (rain), we will start at eight.
2. If the parts ___ (arrive) tomorrow, we will finish on Friday.
3. As soon as she ___ (ring), I will let you know.
4. Provided the site ___ (be) clear, you may begin.
5. I do not know when they ___ (reply).
6. When they ___ (reply), I will tell you.
7. I ___ (ring) you as soon as I hear anything.
8. Assuming nothing ___ (go) wrong, it will be finished by six.
activities.answers:
1. rains  2. arrive  3. rings  4. is  5. will reply  6. reply
7. will ring  8. goes
Number 5 is the exception: that when means at what time, and it is not a condition.
Number 7 is the main half, which is where the will belongs.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Underline the condition word in each one first. The half it opens never takes will.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Match the future to the evidence
activities.instructions:
Choose the best future form for each situation, and write why in three words.
1. The sky is black and you are looking at it.
2. Somebody asks your opinion about next week's weather.
3. You have an appointment on Tuesday at ten.
4. The timetable says six o'clock.
5. The phone rings and you stand up.
6. You decided last week to move the date.
7. It is starting this second.
8. There is a good chance of rain, but you are hedging.
activities.answers:
1. is going to rain — visible evidence
2. will rain — an opinion
3. am meeting — arranged, in a diary
4. is due to arrive — a timetable
5. will get it — decided now
6. are going to move — decided earlier
7. is about to start — any second
8. is likely to rain — probable, hedged
5 and 6 are the pair worth studying: will is decided NOW, going to was decided EARLIER.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the form, then write why you believe it. The reason should choose the form, not the other way round.

activities.title: Practice 4 — With of, or without?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right quantifier phrase.
1. ___ never complain. (people in general)
2. ___ in the room had already left. (that room)
3. ___ read the whole form. (applicants in general, use few)
4. ___ we interviewed were suitable. (the ones we saw, use few)
5. ___ the parts ___ (have) arrived. (not one, use none)
6. ___ applicants applied before the deadline. (not any, use no)
7. ___ disputes arise from condition 3. (use the majority)
8. ___ anybody reads the small print. (almost nobody)
Now correct these.
9. Most of people never complain.
10. The majority people agreed.
activities.answers:
1. Most people  2. Most of the people  3. Few applicants  4. Few of the applicants
5. None of the parts has arrived  6. No applicants  7. The majority of disputes
8. Hardly anybody  9. Most people (or most of THE people)  10. The majority OF people
of and the travel together: you cannot have one without the other.
The majority and none always take of. no never does.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, ask whether you could point at the group. If you could, you need of and the.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Build the noun
activities.instructions:
Write the noun for each word.
1. decide   2. prevent   3. agree     4. apply    5. depend
6. possible 7. aware     8. refer     9. approve  10. commit
11. arrive  12. different
Now rewrite each sentence so the idea is the subject.
13. They decided late, and it cost us.
14. They delayed, and that triggered the review.
15. He was absent, and nobody noticed.
activities.answers:
1. decision  2. prevention  3. agreement  4. application  5. dependence
6. possibility  7. awareness  8. reference  9. approval  10. commitment
11. arrival  12. difference
13. The late decision cost us.  14. The delay triggered the review.
15. His absence went unnoticed.
Watch 4 (y to i), 8 (one r), 10 (one t, unlike committed).
12 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write each pair as verb, then noun. Say both aloud: the stress often moves.

activities.title: Practice 6 — What does the condition actually require?
activities.instructions:
Read each clause and write exactly what somebody must do to satisfy it.
Be precise. Half the point is noticing what the clause does NOT say.
1. The landlord will maintain the system provided it is serviced annually by an approved engineer.
2. The hirer may extend the period provided notice is given before 4pm on the due date.
3. The deposit is refunded as long as the equipment is returned clean and undamaged.
4. Unless the equipment is returned by the due time, a further full day is charged.
5. Damage must be reported on return. Otherwise the full replacement cost is charged.
activities.answers:
1. Have it serviced EVERY year, AND use an engineer from their approved list.
   Both halves, not either. This is the clause from Reading 1.
2. Give notice, before 4pm, on the due date itself. All three.
3. Return it clean AND undamaged. Either failure loses the deposit.
4. Return it by the TIME, not just on the day. This causes most disputes.
5. Report the damage at the moment of return, not later.
4 or 5 right: good. Fewer: read each clause again and count the separate requirements.
activities.solo: Number the separate requirements inside each clause. Most of them hide more than one.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the terms
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 3 only.
1. What must you produce before equipment is released?
2. By what time must you give notice to extend?
3. Which condition causes the majority of disputes?
4. Copy the condition that uses unless, and say what it would be with if not.
5. Copy the sentence that uses none of, and say why the verb is what it is.
6. What happens if the equipment fails and it is not your fault?
activities.answers:
1. Photographic identification.
2. Before 4pm on the due date.
3. Condition 3, the return time.
4. 'Unless the equipment is returned by the due time, a further full day is charged.'
   With if not: If the equipment is not returned by the due time, a further full day is charged.
5. 'None of the items may be taken outside the mainland without written consent.'
   may is a modal, so it does not change form; but none means not one, which is singular.
6. The hire charge is cancelled and a replacement is offered where available.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the terms with a pen and circle every condition word before you answer.

quizzes.q: I will not sign ___ they put it in writing.
quizzes.why: unless means if not, in one word. if would reverse the meaning, and provided is too strong for a refusal.

quizzes.q: Which sentence means the opposite of what the speaker intends?
options: I will not go if they do not invite me.
I will not go unless they do not invite me.
I will not go unless they invite me.
I will go provided they invite me.
quizzes.a: I will not go unless they do not invite me.
quizzes.why: unless already contains the not, so saying it again cancels it. The other three all mean the same thing.

quizzes.q: Unless it ___ , we will start at eight.
quizzes.why: The condition half never takes will, however clearly the sentence is about tomorrow. English marks the future once.

quizzes.q: I will ring you as soon as I ___ anything.
quizzes.why: as soon as opens a condition half, so the present simple is right. The will has already been used in the other half.

quizzes.q: The sky is black and you are looking at it. Which is best?
quizzes.why: going to claims visible evidence, and you have some. will would label it as merely your opinion.

quizzes.q: You have an appointment in the diary for Tuesday. Which is best?
options: I will meet the client on Tuesday.
I am meeting the client on Tuesday.
I am going to meet the client on Tuesday.
I meet the client on Tuesday.
quizzes.a: I am meeting the client on Tuesday.
quizzes.why: The present continuous is for a fixed arrangement, where a time is set and somebody else knows about it too.

quizzes.q: ___ never complain. (you mean people in general)
quizzes.why: A general statement takes no of and no the. Most of the people would mean one particular group you have in mind.

options: The majority of the people agreed with all.
quizzes.why: The majority always takes of, whether the group is general or particular.
In careful writing none means not one, which is singular. You will hear have in speech, but has is what an examiner wants.
The -de becomes -s before the ending. The spelling shift is why this noun has to be learned with its verb.
The y becomes i before the ending. An appliance is a real word, but it means a machine, not the act of applying.

quizzes.q: 'The landlord will maintain it provided it is serviced by an approved engineer.' You had it serviced, but not by an approved engineer. What follows?
options: The landlord must still maintain it.
The condition was partly met, so it is shared.
The condition was not met, so the landlord need not.
quizzes.a: The condition was not met, so the landlord need not.
quizzes.why: provided names the one condition and all of its parts. Meeting half of a condition is not meeting it.

teacherNotes.note: The plan's pattern list here included the SECOND conditional. 7Ug.08 covers zero and first conditionals only; the second conditional is 8Ug.10, placed in Unit 13. Teaching it here would take Unit 13's content and leave that unit hollow. The plan's list has been rewritten to match the codes.

Every card increments something. Zero and first conditionals are L2 U11 and U18; the no-will rule is L2 U18 for when and until only; futures are L1 U11 and L2 U4 and U13, five cards in all; quantifiers are L1 U17 and L2 U6, U14 and U19; abstract nouns are L2 U14 and U16. None of those is re-taught here.
unless + not is the error that reverses meaning, and learners rarely hear it in their own speech. The if-not substitution test in card 1 is the fix; make them apply it aloud every time.
will in the condition half survives well past B1 because both halves genuinely are about the future. State the rule as 'English marks the future once' rather than as a list of six words.
'Most of people' sits exactly between the two correct answers, which is why it is so persistent. of and the travel together; neither appears without the other.

unless, provided, as long as, assuming and otherwise are taught nowhere below this unit, and neither is the evidence-based choice of future form. The quantifier and abstract-noun cards are extensions of existing sets.

Practice 6 is the unit's real assessment of 7Ro.01: it asks the learner to count the separate requirements hidden inside one clause. Reading 1 exists to make that skill feel worth having before the exercise arrives.

selfAssessment.statement: I can use unless without putting not after it.
I know that provided names the one condition, and if only names a condition.
I can keep will out of the half with the condition word in it.
I can choose a future form that matches the evidence I have.
I can say whether I mean people in general or one particular group.
I can build an abstract noun from a verb or an adjective.
I can read a set of conditions and say what each one actually requires.
I can keep my voice up at the comma so a listener knows more is coming.

assignment.title: The conditions, and what they really require
assignment.instructions:
Part one. Write six numbered conditions for something you hire out, lend or agree to.
Use unless, provided, as long as and otherwise at least once each, and state a consequence every time.
Keep will out of every condition half.
Part two. Write a short plan that depends on those conditions, in about eighty words.
Use at least three different future forms, each matched to the evidence you have, and say in
brackets after each one why you chose it.
Part three. Take any TWO of your own conditions and write out every separate requirement
hidden inside them, numbered. Most conditions hide more than one.
Use at least four abstract nouns built from verbs or adjectives across the whole piece.
assignment.submissionType: Written conditions, a plan and a short analysis
